prompt: Which property belongs to gRPC and not to REST with JSON, in section 02's table?
hint: Look at the contract row.

choices.text: Responses that proxies and CDNs store for later
choices.why: That is REST's GET; every gRPC call is a POST that no cache keeps.

choices.text: Messages a person reads straight off the wire with curl
choices.why: That is JSON; protobuf needs the contract to be read.

choices.text: Native calls from fetch inside a web page
choices.why: Browsers reach REST natively and gRPC only through a translator.

choices.text: A contract that both sides are generated from
choices.why: Right. The .proto is required, and clients and servers come out of it.

prompt: How does section 02 say its comparison table should be read?
hint: A score, or something else?

choices.text: As a score: the column with more wins is the better protocol
choices.why: The section says the opposite: neither style is better in general.

choices.text: As questions about who calls the service
choices.why: Right. Browser, mobile app, partner script or your own service decide the answer.

choices.text: As a ranking of speed, since speed decides most choices
choices.why: Section 03 shows speed matters little for a service like boxoffice.

choices.text: As a migration plan from REST to gRPC
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson asks to migrate; boxoffice keeps both.

prompt: Match each row of the table to the style it favours.
hint: Think of browsers, caches and streams.

pairs.left: four kinds of call built in

prompt: How many bytes did 200 events take as raw JSON in cmd/sizes?
hint: The second line of the output.

prompt: And as raw protobuf?
hint: Same line, after JSON.

prompt: Gzipped, 200 events were 1,430 bytes in JSON and 1,350 in protobuf. Why did the gap shrink so much?
hint: What made JSON large in the first place?

choices.text: gzip turns JSON into protobuf on the way
choices.why: Compression changes bytes, not the format; the reader still decompresses JSON.

choices.text: protobuf is already compressed, so gzip adds nothing to it
choices.why: Protobuf also shrank, from 5,671 to 1,350; it is compact, not compressed.

choices.text: gzip removes the repeated key names that made JSON big
choices.why: Right. Repetition is exactly what compression is good at.

choices.text: The program measured the wrong list for protobuf
choices.why: Both encodings carry the same four fields of the same 200 events.

prompt: Two events: JSON 117 bytes raw and 142 gzipped. What does that tell you?
hint: gzip has a fixed cost.

choices.text: JSON compresses badly at every size
choices.why: At 200 events it went from 12,094 to 1,430.

choices.text: gzip's header outweighs a tiny body
choices.why: Right. For small messages the raw difference is the whole difference.

choices.text: The measurement failed
choices.why: Protobuf grew too, 56 to 81: the same effect on both.

choices.text: curl had gzip switched off for that request
choices.why: No curl was involved; cmd/sizes compressed in memory.

prompt: Encoding 200 events took about 27 µs in protobuf and 33 to 35 µs in JSON. Why does the lesson call this irrelevant for boxoffice?
hint: Compare with lesson 6's log.

choices.text: Microbenchmarks give random numbers
choices.why: The two runs agreed closely; the numbers are real, just small.

choices.text: A database query costs milliseconds
choices.why: Right. It matters for a service that only moves messages at very high rates.

choices.text: JSON is faster in production
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson measured that; JSON was slower here.

choices.text: boxoffice encodes nothing on its own
choices.why: Every answer it sends is encoded, as JSON or protobuf.

prompt: cmd/sizes writes the repeated field one tag and length per event with the package ___, which knows the wire format byte by byte.
hint: It is imported from google.golang.org/protobuf/encoding.

prompt: A curl over HTTP/2 to the gRPC port got HTTP/2 200 with grpc-status: 13. What happened to the call?
hint: Where does gRPC put its outcome?

choices.text: It succeeded, as the 200 says
choices.why: Every gRPC call answers 200; the outcome is the grpc-status.

choices.text: curl sent HTTP/1.1, which gRPC refuses with 13
choices.why: That was the second request, which got no usable answer at all; this one spoke HTTP/2.

choices.text: The server sent the status as the HTTP status code, 13
choices.why: HTTP has no status 13; it arrived in a header after the body.

choices.text: It failed with Internal
choices.why: Right. 13 is Internal: the call carried no message at all.

prompt: A team's load balancer reports zero errors on the gRPC service while clients see NotFound and Internal. What explains it?
hint: What does a proxy see when it looks only at HTTP statuses?

choices.text: Errors travel as HTTP 200, grpc-status in a trailer
choices.why: Right. A proxy that only counts HTTP statuses sees every gRPC failure as a success.

choices.text: The balancer drops gRPC errors to save bandwidth
choices.why: Nothing is dropped; the errors arrive, in trailers the balancer does not read.

choices.text: The clients misread success as failure
choices.why: The clients read grpc-status correctly; the balancer does not.

choices.text: NotFound is not an error in gRPC
choices.why: It is one of the status codes, and toStatus sends it for a missing event.

prompt: grpcurl printed event 1 without a "sold" field. Why?
hint: What is sold for event 1?

choices.text: Zero values are left out
choices.why: Right. Event 1 had sold 0, so a reader must know that missing means zero.

choices.text: The server forgot to fill the field
choices.why: GetEvent copies Sold; its value was 0.

choices.text: grpcurl lacked the contract for that field
choices.why: It was given seats.proto with -proto, which declares sold.

choices.text: Reflection was off, so grpcurl showed only some fields
choices.why: Reflection was off, and -proto replaced it fully.

prompt: Why does boxoffice leave gRPC reflection off?
hint: What does reflection give to whoever reaches the port?

choices.text: It slows every call
choices.why: The lesson names no speed cost; the concern is exposure.

choices.text: grpcurl refuses to work with servers that have it
choices.why: The opposite: with it grpcurl needs no .proto.

choices.text: It hands out a map of the API
choices.why: Right. The contract stays in the repository, where clients get it anyway.

choices.text: It needs a second port
choices.why: It is one more service on the same server, registered in one line.

prompt: Order what grpcurl does with -proto and -d for one unary call.
hint: JSON in, JSON out, protobuf between.
items: reads the request written as JSON
encodes it as protobuf using seats.proto
decodes the answer with the same contract
prints the answer back as JSON

prompt: Why can a web page not be a gRPC client of boxoffice as it is?
hint: Two things gRPC needs from HTTP/2.

choices.text: fetch cannot read trailers
choices.why: Right. grpc-status arrives in a trailer, which a page cannot read.

choices.text: Browsers do not speak HTTP/2
choices.why: They do; what they lack is access to trailers and framing.

choices.text: Protobuf cannot be decoded in JavaScript
choices.why: Decoding is possible; the transport is the obstacle.

choices.text: CORS forbids it
choices.why: CORS is about origins; the problem here is the protocol.

prompt: Match each way around the browser problem to what it does.
hint: None was run for the course.

pairs.right: a browser-friendly variant, translated by a proxy such as Envoy
serves gRPC, gRPC-Web and plain JSON from the same handlers
generates a REST and JSON front from annotations in the .proto

right_distractors: compresses protobuf so a browser accepts it

prompt: A company opens an API to partners it will never meet. What does the lesson recommend?
hint: What do all their callers share?

choices.text: gRPC only, since the contract protects them
choices.why: Strangers start with curl; a toolchain first costs adoption.

choices.text: GraphQL, because the lesson compares three styles
choices.why: The lesson compares REST and gRPC only.

choices.text: Whatever the internal services use, for consistency
choices.why: The choice follows the callers, and these callers are strangers.

choices.text: REST and JSON with an OpenAPI description
choices.why: Right. Clients can still be generated, without gRPC's tooling.

prompt: A public catalogue of events is read by thousands of visitors. Which property of REST matters most here?
hint: Who can answer instead of the server?

choices.text: Its smaller size on the wire
choices.why: JSON is the larger of the two raw.

choices.text: Its deadlines
choices.why: Deadlines are gRPC's strength.

choices.text: A GET is cacheable
choices.why: Right. Every gRPC call is a POST that no cache stores.

choices.text: Its generated clients in every language
choices.why: That is gRPC's row; REST needs OpenAPI for it.

prompt: Why did an HTTP purchase reach a gRPC watcher half a second later?
hint: Two adapters, one core.

choices.text: Both doors call one store and one table
choices.why: Right. A sale is the same Sell whichever door it came through.

choices.text: The HTTP handler calls the gRPC server
choices.why: The adapters never call each other; both call the store.

choices.text: gRPC copies the HTTP log
choices.why: Watch reads the event from the store every half-second.

choices.text: PostgreSQL pushes the change to gRPC clients
choices.why: Nothing pushes; Watch polls the store on a ticker.

prompt: Match each caller to its door in boxoffice.
hint: Browsers, staff scripts, programs the venue owns.

prompt: What does serving both doors cost, according to section 06?
hint: Think of what cuts across requests.

choices.text: Two copies of the store, kept in sync by a job
choices.why: There is one store; that is the point of the pattern.

choices.text: Cross-cutting code, twice
choices.why: Right. Logging, metrics, authentication and errors exist in both shapes.

choices.text: A second database for gRPC
choices.why: Both share one pool and one PostgreSQL.

choices.text: Business rules duplicated in each adapter
choices.why: The adapters contain no business rule; the store does.

prompt: Put section 07's four questions in the order the lesson asks them.
hint: The first one decides REST on its own.
items: Is the caller a browser, or a stranger's program?
Do you own both ends, for years?

prompt: Two services of the same team will exchange a few hundred requests a minute for years, no browser involved, no streaming. What does the lesson's reasoning lead to?
hint: Which of the four questions is yes?

choices.text: gRPC, for the required contract
choices.why: Right. A renamed field breaks the build of every client instead of production.

choices.text: REST, because the volume is low
choices.why: Volume is only the fourth question; the second one is already yes.

choices.text: gRPC-Web, to keep a browser option open
choices.why: No browser is involved; a translator would be pure cost.

choices.text: Both doors from day one
choices.why: Section 06 says not to add a second protocol before a caller needs it.

prompt: Which are signs, per section 07, that gRPC was the wrong choice? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three of them are listed for gRPC.

choices.text: every caller goes through a gateway back to JSON
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: most debugging starts by installing grpcurl
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: a browser client is the main user
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: polling loops imitate streams everywhere
choices.why: That is a sign REST was the wrong choice.

choices.text: hand-written client structs drift from the server's
choices.why: Also a sign against REST, which has no required contract.

prompt: If none of the four questions is yes, what does the lesson recommend, and why?
hint: Lesson 5's default.

choices.text: gRPC, since it is newer
choices.why: Age is not one of the criteria.

choices.text: REST, the simpler one
choices.why: Right. Simplicity is the default lesson 5 argued for.

choices.text: Both, to be safe
choices.why: Two doors write every cross-cutting concern twice.

choices.text: Whichever the framework of lesson 4 prefers
choices.why: The choice follows the callers, not a framework.

prompt: A mobile app of your own shows a live seat count and must work on a train with patchy signal. Which door, from what the lesson argued?
hint: You own both ends, and the conversation is a stream.

choices.text: gRPC, for server streaming with deadlines on each call
choices.why: Right. Questions 2 and 3 are yes, and no browser is involved.

choices.text: REST, because mobile apps are browsers
choices.why: A native app is a program with its own HTTP/2 client, not a web page.

choices.text: REST, because protobuf is larger on bad networks
choices.why: Protobuf was the smaller of the two in every measurement.

choices.text: Neither: a live count needs a CDN
choices.why: A CDN caches; a live count changes with every sale.

prompt: A colleague proposes moving boxoffice's public HTTP API to gRPC to save bandwidth. Which measurement answers them?
hint: Answers are compressed.

choices.text: 12,094 against 5,671 bytes raw
choices.why: Raw is not what travels when HTTP compresses its answers.

choices.text: 27 µs against 33 µs to encode
choices.why: That is speed, not bandwidth, and it is dwarfed by the database.

choices.text: 1,430 against 1,350 bytes gzipped
choices.why: Right. About six per cent, and the public callers would lose curl and caches.

choices.text: 56 against 117 bytes for two events
choices.why: A list of two is not a public catalogue, and both grew when gzipped.
